title: Joining a round
subtitle: The slip-stitch join and the invisible join
excerpt: When you crochet in the round, each round has to be closed back into a ring. The plain slip-stitch join is quick and works everywhere; the invisible join hides the seam for a smoother finish on the last round. This covers both.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passages on working in rounds and closing each round (the crochet square and medallion worked in rounds, Fig. 441). Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The invisible join is a modern refinement of the same closing principle.

glossaryTerms.definition: Closing a round by working a slip stitch into the top of the first stitch of that round, which links the end of the round back to its start.
A neater way to close the final round, where the cut tail is threaded through the first and last stitches to mimic the top of a stitch, hiding the seam.
A blunt large-eyed needle used to weave in ends and to sew yarn seams. Its blunt tip slides between strands without splitting them.

content.text: When you work in the round, each round comes back to where it began and has to be closed into a ring before the next one starts. The everyday way is the
slip-stitch join
, which is quick and works on every round. For the very last round, an
invisible join
hides the small step the slip stitch leaves, for a smoother edge on a finished motif.
What you need
A piece worked in the round in DK yarn, partway through, to practise the slip-stitch join.
A 4 mm hook.
One tapestry needle and scissors for the invisible join on the final round.
The slip-stitch join
Work all the stitches of the round as the pattern sets them out.
Find the first stitch of the round. On a treble round this is the top of the beginning chain that stood in for the first stitch.
Insert the hook into the top of that first stitch.
Wrap the yarn over and draw it through the stitch and the loop on the hook in one pull. The round is now closed.
You will know the join is right when the round forms a continuous ring with no gap, and the stitch count still matches the pattern.
The invisible join
Finish the last stitch of the final round, then cut the yarn leaving a 12 cm tail.
Pull the tail all the way through the last loop so the work cannot unravel.
Thread the tail onto the tapestry needle. Pass the needle under both loops of the first stitch of the round, then back down into the top of the last stitch.
Adjust the tension until the new loop matches the size of the stitches around it, then weave the tail in on the back.
You will know it has worked when the join looks like one more stitch in the round rather than a stepped seam.
Common mistakes
Joining into the wrong stitch. It is easy to slip stitch into the second stitch by mistake, which shifts the start of every round. Count back to the true first stitch each time.
Pulling the slip stitch tight. A tight join puckers the ring. Keep it as loose as the stitches around it.
Using an invisible join on a middle round. Save it for the last round; mid-piece it just adds bulk.
When to use it
Use the slip-stitch join on any joined round of a motif, a hat brim, or a granny square. Use the
tapestry needle

and the invisible join on the final round of anything where the edge shows, such as a coaster, a doily, or the outer round of a blanket. Spiral work, like amigurumi, skips joins entirely and just keeps going round.
